claim: During parasitoid wasp infection, activated immune cells of Drosophila melanogaster larvae release adenosine to conserve nutrients for immune response.
source: During parasitoid wasp infection, activated immune cells of Drosophila melanogaster larvae release adenosine to conserve nutrients for immune response.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known finding from previous work.

claim: S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) is a methyl group donor for most methylations in the cell and is synthesized from methionine and ATP.
source: S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) is a methyl group donor for most methylations in the cell and is synthesized from methionine and ATP.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge stated in the abstract.

claim: After methylation, SAM is converted to S-adenosylhomocysteine, which is further metabolized to adenosine and homocysteine.
source: After methylation, SAM is converted to S-adenosylhomocysteine, which is further metabolized to adenosine and homocysteine.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge stated in the abstract.

claim: The SAM transmethylation pathway is up-regulated during immune cell activation.
source: Here, we show that the SAM transmethylation pathway is up-regulated during immune cell activation
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data including metabolomics and gene expression analysis.

claim: Adenosine produced by the SAM transmethylation pathway in immune cells acts as a systemic signal to delay Drosophila larval development.
source: the adenosine produced by this pathway in immune cells acts as a systemic signal to delay Drosophila larval development and ensure sufficient nutrient supply to the immune system.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by developmental timing experiments and RNAi knockdown studies.

claim: The up-regulation of the SAM transmethylation pathway depends on the recycling of adenosine back to ATP by adenosine kinase and adenylate kinase.
source: We further show that the up-regulation of the SAM transmethylation pathway and the efficiency of the immune response also depend on the recycling of adenosine back to ATP by adenosine kinase and adenylate kinase.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by RNAi knockdown experiments and isotope tracing studies.

claim: The efficiency of the immune response depends on the recycling of adenosine back to ATP by adenosine kinase and adenylate kinase.
source: We further show that the up-regulation of the SAM transmethylation pathway and the efficiency of the immune response also depend on the recycling of adenosine back to ATP by adenosine kinase and adenylate kinase.
evidence: This is supported by survival and lamellocyte production data in RNAi knockdown experiments.

claim: Adenosine may act as a sensitive sensor of the balance between cell activity (represented by the sum of methylation events) and nutrient supply.
source: We therefore hypothesize that adenosine may act as a sensitive sensor of the balance between cell activity, represented by the sum of methylation events in the cell, and nutrient supply.
evidence: This is presented as a hypothesis based on the experimental findings.

claim: If the supply of nutrients is insufficient for a given activity, adenosine may not be effectively recycled back into ATP and may be pushed out of the cell to serve as a signal to demand more nutrients.
source: If the supply of nutrients is insufficient for a given activity, adenosine may not be effectively recycled back into ATP and may be pushed out of the cell to serve as a signal to demand more nutrients.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism proposed based on the findings.

claim: Immune cells produce cytokines Upd2 and Upd3, which induce the production of the insulin signaling inhibitor Impl2 in muscle tissue via the Jak/Stat signaling pathway.
source: For example, we have recently shown that immune cells produce cytokines Upd2 and Upd3, which induce the production of the insulin signaling inhibitor Impl2 in muscle tissue via the Jak/Stat signaling pathway.
evidence: This is cited as previous work from the authors' group.

claim: Impl2 reduces the consumption of carbohydrates by muscle, making nutrients more available to immune cells.
source: Impl2 reduces the consumption of carbohydrates by muscle, making nutrients more available to immune cells (McMullen et al., 2024).
evidence: This is cited from a specific reference.

claim: Extracellular adenosine signaling, through the adenosine receptor, reduces nutrient consumption by non-immune tissues and slows the development of the organism.
source: Extracellular adenosine signaling, through the adenosine receptor, reduces nutrient consumption by non-immune tissues and slows the development of the organism, again leaving more nutrients available for the immune system (Bajgar et al., 2015; Dolezal, 2015; Bajgar and Dolezal, 2018).
evidence: This is cited from previous work.

claim: The bacterium Myxococcus xanthus responds to nutrient depletion by releasing adenosine, which initiates the aggregation of bacteria into fruiting bodies.
source: For example, the bacterium Myxococcus xanthus responds to nutrient depletion by releasing adenosine, which initiates the aggregation of bacteria into fruiting bodies (Shimkets and Dworkin, 1981).
evidence: This is cited from a specific reference.

claim: In mammals, heart muscles secrete adenosine during ischemia, which causes blood vessels to dilate to increase blood flow and delivery of oxygen and nutrients.
source: In mammals, the heart muscles secrete adenosine during ischemia, which causes blood vessels to dilate to increase blood flow and delivery of oxygen and nutrients (Lloyd et al., 1988; Deussen et al., 1989; Kroll et al., 1992; Reiss et al., 2019).
evidence: This is cited from multiple references.

claim: Adenosine plays an important role in the induction of sleep, torpor and hibernation, physiological states associated with energy conservation.
source: Adenosine also plays an important role in the induction of sleep, torpor and hibernation, physiological states associated with energy conservation (Fredholm et al., 2011; Boison and Jarvis, 2021).
evidence: This is cited from specific references.

claim: Adenosine is produced intracellularly in two ways: by conversion from AMP by nucleotidases or in the SAM transmethylation pathway from S-adenosylhomocysteine by S-adenosylhomocysteinase (Ahcy).
source: Adenosine is produced intracellularly in two ways (Figure 1), by conversion from AMP by nucleotidases or in the S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) transmethylation pathway from S-adenosylhomocysteine (SAH) by S-adenosylhomocysteinase (Ahcy).
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Increased AMP activates AMPK, which suppresses energy-consuming processes in the cell and activates energy-producing processes.
source: Increased AMP activates AMPK, which suppresses energy-consuming processes in the cell and activates energy-producing processes (Kloor and Osswald, 2004; Dzeja and Terzic, 2009).
evidence: This is cited from specific references.

claim: AMP is converted by nucleotidases to adenosine, which is released from the cell via the equilibrative nucleoside transporter (ENT).
source: AMP is also converted by nucleotidases to adenosine, which is released from the cell via the equilibrative nucleoside transporter (ENT), where it signals the metabolic stress of the cell to surrounding cells and tissues via adenosine receptors (Dolezelova et al., 2007; Fenckova et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from specific references.

claim: Activated AMPK suppresses the function of immune cells.
source: Since activated AMPK suppresses the function of immune cells (Salminen et al., 2011)
evidence: This is cited from a specific reference.

claim: SAH must be rapidly converted to homocysteine and adenosine, or it will block further methylation.
source: After the methyl group is transferred to the target molecule by methyltransferase, SAM becomes SAH, which must be rapidly converted to homocysteine and adenosine, or it will block further methylation.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge.

claim: As methylation increases in the cell, more SAM is formed and at the same time SAH is cleared more rapidly, leading to an increase in the SAM:SAH ratio, known as the methylation index.
source: As methylation increases in the cell, more SAM is formed and at the same time SAH is cleared more rapidly, leading to an increase in the SAM:SAH ratio, known as the methylation index.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge.

claim: For the 'SAM to homocysteine + adenosine' direction to prevail, homocysteine and adenosine must be metabolized or excreted from the cell very rapidly.
source: SAH is converted to homocysteine and adenosine by Ahcy, which works in both directions; for the 'SAM to homocysteine +adenosine' direction to prevail, homocysteine and adenosine must also be metabolized or excreted from the cell very rapidly (Lu, 2000; Kloor and Osswald, 2004; Yu et al., 2019; Roy et al., 2020; Vizán et al., 2021).
evidence: This is cited from multiple references.

claim: Homocysteine can either be recycled back to methionine, or further metabolized in the transsulfuration pathway.
source: Homocysteine can either be recycled back to methionine, or further metabolized in the transsulfuration pathway (source of cysteine, H2S, and antioxidants) (Sbodio et al., 2019).
evidence: This is cited from a specific reference.

claim: Adenosine can be catabolized to inosine by adenosine deaminase.
source: Adenosine can be catabolized to inosine by adenosine deaminase (Novakova and Dolezal, 2011)
evidence: This is cited from a specific reference.

claim: Adenosine can be recycled to AMP by adenosine kinase and further to ATP by adenylate kinase, glycolysis or oxidative phosphorylation.
source: or recycled to AMP by adenosine kinase and further to ATP by adenylate kinase, glycolysis or oxidative phosphorylation (Zeleznikar et al., 1990; Zeleznikar et al., 1995; Dzeja et al., 2007; Dzeja and Terzic, 2009).
evidence: This is cited from multiple references.

claim: The importance of adenosine recycling to AMP by adenosine kinase is indicated by the dependence of the methylation cycle on the concomitant function of this enzyme.
source: The importance of adenosine recycling to AMP by adenosine kinase is indicated by the dependence of the methylation cycle on the concomitant function of this enzyme (Lecoq et al., 2001; Bjursell et al., 2011; Moffatt et al., 2002).
evidence: This is cited from multiple references.

claim: Every single methylation in the cell is associated with the formation of one adenosine molecule.
source: Since every single methylation in the cell is associated with the formation of one adenosine molecule, the amount of adenosine accurately reflects the intensity of the SAM transmethylation pathway.
evidence: This is based on biochemical knowledge of the SAM transmethylation pathway.

claim: The amount of adenosine accurately reflects the intensity of the SAM transmethylation pathway.
source: Since every single methylation in the cell is associated with the formation of one adenosine molecule, the amount of adenosine accurately reflects the intensity of the SAM transmethylation pathway.
evidence: This is an inference based on biochemical knowledge.

claim: The SAM transmethylation pathway is upregulated and has critical function in mammalian immune cells.
source: Given its upregulation and critical function in mammalian immune cells (Lawson et al., 2012; Yu et al., 2019; Roy et al., 2020)
evidence: This is cited from multiple references.

claim: Putative methionine transporters and all enzymes of the SAM transmethylation pathway are strongly expressed in hemocytes, both in the resting and activated state.
source: Putative methionine transporters, as well as all enzymes of this pathway, are strongly expressed in hemocytes, both in the resting and activated state (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 1—source data 1 and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 2B and supplementary materials.

claim: The expression of mnd and gb methionine transporters is particularly high and is further increased during infection.
source: The expression of mnd and gb is particularly high and is further increased during infection (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 43 methyltransferases significantly increased their expression in both 9 and 18 hpi.
source: We found that 43 methyltransferases (at least 24 of them categorized as SAM-dependent methyltransferases) significantly increased their expression in both 9 and 18 hpi (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Ahcy shows the highest expression among SAM transmethylation pathway enzymes.
source: Ahcy (Ahcy; CG11654; EC 3.3.1.1; FBgn0014455) hydrolyzes SAH into adenosine and homocysteine and shows the highest expression among SAM transmethylation pathway enzymes (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: AhcyL1 and AhcyL2, which work as dominant-negative regulators of Ahcy, have a lower expression and are downregulated during infection.
source: AhcyL1 (CG9977; FBgn0035371) and AhcyL2 (CG8956; FBgn0015011), which work as dominant-negative regulators of Ahcy Parkhitko et al., 2016 have a lower expression and are downregulated during infection (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 2B and cited reference.

claim: In control larvae, the labeled intracellular methionine fraction reached almost 70% in resting hemocytes and over 80% in activated hemocytes after 20 min of ex vivo incubation.
source: In control larvae, the labeled intracellular methionine fraction reached almost 70% in resting hemocytes and over 80% in activated hemocytes after 20 min of ex vivo incubation, demonstrating a substantial uptake of methionine into hemocytes (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by isotope tracing data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: There is a twofold increase of SAM and SAH in infected compared to control animals.
source: Much of this methionine is used for SAM production and methylation, as indicated by the twofold increase of SAM and SAH in infected compared to control animals (Figure 2D and E); demonstrating an upregulation of the SAM transmethylation pathway in activated hemocytes.
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figures 2D and E.

claim: There is a significantly higher methylation index (ratio of SAM:SAH) in activated hemocytes.
source: This is further supported by a significantly higher methylation index (ratio of SAM:SAH; Figure 2H–J) in activated hemocytes.
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figures 2H-J.

claim: The m+4 portion of the labeled methionine did not exceed the 3% threshold, indicating that methionine used for the SAM transmethylation pathway in hemocytes is derived from hemolymph and homocysteine is not remethylated to methionine.
source: However, the m+4 portion of the labeled methionine (m+4 and m+5) did not exceed the 3% threshold, set by the methionine labeling impurity (ratio 'm+4/[m+4 + m+5]' in the medium was 3%; Figure 2F). This indicates that methionine used for the SAM transmethylation pathway in hemocytes is derived from hemolymph and homocysteine is not remethylated to methionine.
evidence: This is supported by isotope tracing data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Ahcy RNAi leads to reduced 13C-labeled methionine uptake in resting hemocytes, although uptake is still increased upon infection.
source: Ahcy RNAi leads to reduced 13C-labeled methionine uptake in resting hemocytes, although uptake is still increased upon infection (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by isotope tracing data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Methionine incorporation into SAM is significantly lower in activated hemocytes with Ahcy RNAi.
source: Methionine incorporation into SAM is significantly lower in activated hemocytes (Figure 2D)
evidence: This is supported by isotope tracing data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Incorporation into SAH is decreased in both quiescent and activated hemocytes with Ahcy RNAi.
source: and incorporation into SAH is decreased in both, quiescent and activated hemocytes (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by isotope tracing data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: SAH is heavily accumulated in Ahcy RNAi hemocytes.
source: This is reflected in metabolite levels, where SAH is heavily accumulated in Ahcy RNAi hemocytes (Figure 2I)
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: SAM and methionine levels are higher in Ahcy RNAi hemocytes compared to controls.
source: and SAM and methionine levels are higher compared to controls (Figure 2G and H); indicating that they are not metabolized in the SAM transmethylation pathway.
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figures 2G and H.

claim: The methylation index in Ahcy RNAi hemocytes is very low compared to controls, and does not increase upon infection.
source: This is substantiated by a methylation index that is very low compared to controls, and does not increase upon infection (Figure 2J).
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: There is significantly higher incorporation of 13C methionine into MTA in activated hemocytes.
source: There is significantly higher incorporation of 13 C methionine into MTA in activated hemocytes (Figure 2K) with no changes in MTA level (Figure 2L).
evidence: This is supported by isotope tracing and metabolomics data shown in Figures 2K and L.

claim: Ahcy RNAi hemocytes have increased MTA levels.
source: Ahcy RNAi hemocytes have increased MTA levels (Figure 2L), which can reflect MTA accumulation, due to decreased SAM transmethylation pathway activity.
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 2L.

claim: There is notable 13C methionine incorporation into CTH.
source: This is supported by notable 13 C methionine incorporation into CTH (Figure 2M).
evidence: This is supported by isotope tracing data shown in Figure 2M.

claim: There is a small, but significant, drop in the labeled CTH fraction in activated hemocytes.
source: Interestingly, there is a small, but significant, drop in the labeled CTH fraction in activated hemocytes (Figure 2M), however, this could be due to an overall increase in the level of CTH, including the unlabeled form (Figure 2N).
evidence: This is supported by isotope tracing and metabolomics data shown in Figures 2M and N.

claim: Cbs expression in Drosophila larval hemocytes is rather low, and even decreases during infection.
source: Based on our transcriptomic data, Cbs expression in Drosophila larval hemocytes is rather low, and even decreases during infection.
evidence: This is based on RNAseq data.

claim: Cystathionine γ-lyase is strongly expressed in hemocytes, at similar levels to Ahcy.
source: Interestingly, cystathionine γ-lyase is strongly expressed, at similar levels to Ahcy.
evidence: This is based on RNAseq data.

claim: Homocysteine is cleared by cystathionine γ-lyase and H2S production rather than via CTH and Cbs.
source: Therefore, our data gives evidence to the clearance of homocysteine by cystathionine γ-lyase and H2S production rather than via CTH and Cbs.
evidence: This is an inference based on gene expression data.

claim: There is an alternative connection of methionine with homocysteine and consequently CTH, in addition to Ahcy.
source: This suggests, there is an alternative connection of methionine with homocysteine and consequently CTH, in addition to Ahcy.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that CTH levels remain normal in Ahcy RNAi hemocytes.

claim: Activated hemocytes release increased amount of adenosine.
source: In our previous work, we showed that activated hemocytes release increased amount of adenosine (Bajgar et al., 2015; Bajgar and Dolezal, 2018).
evidence: This is cited from previous work.

claim: Adenosine release from activated hemocytes causes a systemic metabolic switch that slows the organism's development.
source: This causes a systemic metabolic switch that slows the organism's development, leaving energy for an effective immune response.
evidence: This is cited from previous work.

claim: There is a significant reduction in intracellular adenosine levels after infection.
source: This appears to be reflected in the significant reduction in intracellular adenosine levels after infection (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Extracellular adenosine levels increase after infection.
source: since extracellular adenosine levels increase after infection (Figure 3B)
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The level of inosine increases after infection.
source: as does the level of inosine, which is formed from adenosine by the action of the adenosine deaminase ADGF-A.
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data.

claim: Hemocyte-specific Ahcy RNAi leads to a significant decrease in intracellular adenosine levels.
source: Hemocyte-specific Ahcy RNAi leads to a significant decrease in intracellular adenosine levels, confirming that a significant fraction of adenosine is generated by the SAM transmethylation pathway (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: There is no increase in extracellular adenosine, or inosine levels upon Ahcy knockdown in hemocytes following infection.
source: However, there is no increase in extracellular adenosine, or inosine levels upon Ahcy knockdown in hemocytes following infection (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Silencing of Ahcy in hemocytes during infection leads to a significant reduction (by 6 hr) in developmental delay.
source: This is further supported by the fact that silencing of Ahcy in hemocytes during infection leads to a significant reduction (by 6 hr) in developmental delay (Figure 3C)
evidence: This is supported by developmental timing data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Ahcy RNAi in hemocytes results in diminished host defense, which is associated with reduced production of lamellocytes and encapsulation of the parasitoid.
source: Similar to our previous work (Bajgar et al., 2015), this results in diminished host defense, which is associated with reduced production of lamellocytes and encapsulation of the parasitoid (Figure 3D) and reduced survival (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by lamellocyte counts, encapsulation efficiency, and survival data shown in Figures 3D and E.

claim: The induction of Ahcy RNAi in hemocytes accelerates development by approximately 2 hr, even in the absence of infection.
source: Interestingly, the induction of Ahcy RNAi in hemocytes accelerates development by approximately 2 hr, even in the absence of infection (Figure 3C)
evidence: This is supported by developmental timing data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The normal activity of hemocytes, associated with methylation and adenosine release, appears to slow the overall development of the organism.
source: The normal activity of hemocytes, associated with methylation and adenosine release, appears to slow the overall development of the organism.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Ahcy RNAi accelerates development even without infection.

claim: Activated immune cells have active de novo purine production.
source: Therefore, activated immune cells have active de novo purine production, as shown in mammalian macrophages and T lymphocytes (Yu et al., 2019; Roy et al., 2020).
evidence: This is cited from specific references.

claim: Recent work showed increased pentose phosphate pathway activity is linked with nucleotide production in activated hemocytes.
source: Our recent work showed increased pentose phosphate pathway activity is linked with nucleotide production in activated hemocytes (Kazek et al., 2024).
evidence: This is cited from a specific reference.

claim: Ahcy activity has been linked to adenosine kinase activity, which produces AMP from Ado.
source: Ahcy activity has indeed been linked to adenosine kinase activity, which produces AMP from Ado (Moffatt et al., 2002; Xu et al., 2017; Murugan et al., 2021).
evidence: This is cited from multiple references.

claim: The most striking expression change detected in activated hemocytes was the increase of adenosine kinase Adk3.
source: The most striking expression change we detected in activated hemocytes was the increase of adenosine kinase Adk3 (Figure 4B and C)
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq and qPCR data shown in Figures 4B and C.

claim: Cytosolic adenylate kinase Ak1 expression increases in activated hemocytes.
source: and cytosolic adenylate kinase Ak1 (Figure 4B and D).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq and qPCR data shown in Figures 4B and D.

claim: Another adenosine kinase, Adk2, which is not altered by infection, is also highly expressed in hemocytes.
source: Another adenosine kinase, Adk2, which is not altered by infection, is also highly expressed in hemocytes, as is the mitochondrial adenylate kinase Ak2 (Figure 4B–D).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq and qPCR data shown in Figures 4B-D.

claim: The increase of cytosolic Ak1 indicates at least partial redirection of energy metabolism from mitochondria (oxidative phosphorylation) into cytosol (aerobic glycolysis) in activated immune cells.
source: The increase of cytosolic Ak1 indicates at least partial redirection of energy metabolism from mitochondria (oxidative phosphorylation) into cytosol (aerobic glycolysis) in activated immune cells (Kornberg, 2020).
evidence: This is an inference based on gene expression data and cited reference.

claim: The increase in all levels of IMP, AMP, ADP, and ATP indicates that de novo nucleotide production occurs in activated hemocytes.
source: The increase in all levels of IMP, AMP, ADP, and ATP (Figure 4E–H) indicates that de novo nucleotide production occurs in activated hemocytes.
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figures 4E-H.

claim: Hemocytes recycle adenosine to ATP.
source: This demonstrates that hemocytes recycle adenosine to ATP, in addition to de novo purine synthesis.
evidence: This is supported by isotope tracing experiments.

claim: Both the AMP m+5 and ATP m+5 fractions are lower after infection.
source: Both the AMP m+5 and ATP m+5 fractions are lower after infection (Figure 4I and J).
evidence: This is supported by isotope tracing data shown in Figures 4I and J.

claim: Resting hemocytes show a diminished fraction of labeled SAM derived from labeled adenosine.
source: Resting hemocytes show a diminished fraction of labeled SAM derived from labeled adenosine (Figure 4K).
evidence: This is supported by isotope tracing data shown in Figure 4K.

claim: After infection, there is a significant increase in SAM labeling from adenosine.
source: After infection, there is a significant increase in SAM labeling (Figure 4K), with approximately 13% of labeled ATP molecules being used for SAM synthesis (compare Figure 4J to Figure 4K)
evidence: This is supported by isotope tracing data shown in Figures 4J and K.

claim: A higher fraction of labeled SAM in activated hemocytes suggests a physical connection of SAM synthesis and ATP recycling from labeled adenosine.
source: A higher fraction of labeled SAM in activated hemocytes suggests a physical connection of SAM synthesis and ATP recycling from labeled adenosine.
evidence: This is an inference based on isotope tracing data.

claim: Adk3 RNAi reduces the infection-induced increase in expression almost eight times.
source: Adk3 RNAi reduces the infection-induced increase in expression almost eight times (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: There is significantly lower level of AMP in hemocytes from the infected larvae with Adk3 RNAi.
source: However, there is significantly lower level of AMP in hemocytes from the infected larvae (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Increase in methylation index is abrogated upon Adk3 RNAi.
source: Increase in methylation index is abrogated upon Adk3 RNAi (Figure 5B), showing that Adk3 activity is required for the infection-induced increase in SAM transmethylation pathway.
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The consequences of Adk3 knockdown phenocopy those of Ahcy knockdown animals, as development is significantly less delayed during infection.
source: The consequences of Adk3 knockdown phenocopy those of Ahcy knockdown animals, as development is significantly less delayed during infection (Figure 5C)
evidence: This is supported by developmental timing data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Number of lamellocytes is decreased with Adk3 RNAi.
source: and number of lamellocytes (Figure 5D), as well as survival (Figure 5E) are decreased.
evidence: This is supported by lamellocyte counts shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Survival is decreased with Adk3 RNAi.
source: and number of lamellocytes (Figure 5D), as well as survival (Figure 5E) are decreased.
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The methylation index is abrogated upon cytoplasmic Ak1 knockdown.
source: The methylation index is abrogated (Figure 5B)
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Development is significantly less delayed during infection upon Ak1 RNAi-mediated knockdown.
source: development is significantly less delayed during infection (Figure 5F)
evidence: This is supported by developmental timing data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Number of lamellocytes is decreased upon Ak1 RNAi.
source: number of lamellocytes is decreased (Figure 5G) and survival is lower (Figure 5H) upon Ak1 RNAi-mediated knockdown.
evidence: This is supported by lamellocyte counts shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Survival is lower upon Ak1 RNAi.
source: number of lamellocytes is decreased (Figure 5G) and survival is lower (Figure 5H) upon Ak1 RNAi-mediated knockdown.
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Recycling of adenosine to AMP and potentially to ATP and SAM, using adenosine kinase and cytoplasmic adenylate kinase, appears to be important for activated hemocytes to increase the SAM transmethylation pathway and for effective immune response.
source: In summary, recycling of adenosine to AMP and potentially to ATP and SAM, using adenosine kinase and cytoplasmic adenylate kinase, appears to be important for activated hemocytes to increase the SAM transmethylation pathway and for effective immune response.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the RNAi experiments.

claim: LPS-activated macrophages synergistically increase glycolysis, one carbon metabolism, serine synthesis pathway, pentose phosphate pathway, de novo purine synthesis, and SAM transmethylation pathway activity.
source: It has been shown that LPS-activated macrophages synergistically increase glycolysis, one carbon metabolism, serine synthesis pathway, pentose phosphate pathway, de novo purine synthesis, and SAM transmethylation pathway activity, to induce, and maintain a proinflammatory phenotype.
evidence: This is cited knowledge from mammalian studies.

claim: The homocysteine produced by LPS-activated macrophages is not recycled back into methionine, but SAM synthesis is likely fed exclusively with exogenous methionine transported into the cells.
source: Interestingly, the homocysteine produced by these macrophages is not recycled back into methionine, but SAM synthesis is likely fed exclusively with exogenous methionine transported into the cells (Yu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is cited from a specific reference.

claim: Methionine is a crucial metabolite in driving T cells proinflammatory phenotype via epigenetic reprogramming.
source: They identified methionine as a crucial metabolite in driving T cells proinflammatory phenotype via epigenetic reprogramming and demonstrated dietary methionine restriction as an effective intervention for autoimmune disease.
evidence: This is cited knowledge from mammalian studies.

claim: Activated T lymphocytes upregulate glycolysis, serine, glycine, and one-carbon metabolism including the SAM transmethylation pathway.
source: Activated T lymphocytes, like macrophages, upregulate glycolysis, serine, glycine, and one-carbon metabolism including the SAM transmethylation pathway.
evidence: This is cited knowledge from mammalian studies.

claim: In activated T lymphocytes, the folate cycle and the SAM transmethylation pathway are uncoupled and homocysteine is not remethylated.
source: These studies indicated that the folate cycle and the SAM transmethylation pathway are uncoupled and homocysteine is not remethylated.
evidence: This is cited knowledge from mammalian studies.

claim: In activated T lymphocytes, SAM is synthesized from exogenous methionine and ATP, predominantly produced by de novo purine synthesis.
source: Importantly, SAM is synthesized from exogenous methionine and ATP, predominantly produced by de novo purine synthesis.
evidence: This is cited knowledge from mammalian studies.

claim: In Drosophila immune cells, SAM is synthesized mostly from exogenous methionine, and homocysteine is not remethylated back to methionine, but rather used in transsulfuration pathway.
source: Here, we show that in Drosophila immune cells, SAM is also synthesized mostly from exogenous methionine, and homocysteine is not remethylated back to methionine, but rather used in transsulfuration pathway.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by isotope tracing data.

claim: Ahcy was shown to play an important role in adenosine production in heart muscle cells, under normoxic conditions.
source: Ahcy was shown to play an important role in adenosine production in heart muscle cells, under normoxic conditions (Lloyd et al., 1988; Deussen et al., 1989).
evidence: This is cited from specific references.

claim: Adenosine produced by Ahcy contributes to viability of hepatocellular carcinoma cells (HepG2).
source: Adenosine produced by Ahcy contributes to viability of hepatocellular carcinoma cells (HepG2), since Ahcy knockdown followed by adenosine depletion leads to activation of the DNA damage response, cell cycle arrest, a decreased proliferation rate and DNA damage (Belužić et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited from a specific reference.

claim: Knockdown of Ahcy by RNAi suppresses the infection-induced increase in extracellular adenosine.
source: Knockdown of Ahcy by RNAi suppresses the infection-induced increase in extracellular adenosine, as well as the delay in development, demonstrating that this important systemic signal is most likely generated by the SAM transmethylation pathway.
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics and developmental timing data.

claim: Ectoenzymes are an important source of extracellular adenosine that convert extracellular ATP to ADP, AMP, and adenosine.
source: Ectoenzymes are an important source of extracellular adenosine that convert extracellular ATP to ADP, AMP, and adenosine. This cascade is an important immunomodulator in mammals (Antonioli et al., 2022).
evidence: This is cited from a specific reference.

claim: Drosophila has a cascade of ectoenzymes, which appears not to have an immunomodulatory role, likely due to more rudimentary adenosine signaling.
source: Drosophila also has this cascade of ectoenzymes (Fenckova et al., 2011), which appears not to have an immunomodulatory role, likely due to more rudimentary adenosine signaling (Dolezelova et al., 2007)
evidence: This is cited from specific references.

claim: The ineffective immune response in Ahcy RNAi animals is at least in part due to suppression of the SAM transmethylation pathway itself in hemocytes, which is required for their function.
source: It is also important to add that while adenosine-mediated metabolic suppression and developmental delay are important for an effective immune response, it is likely that the ineffective immune response in Ahcy RNAi animals is at least in part due to suppression of the SAM transmethylation pathway itself in hemocytes, which is required for their function.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results.

claim: After ATP, SAM is the most used substrate in the cell, with up to half of the daily methionine intake in humans used for SAM synthesis.
source: After ATP, SAM is the most used substrate in the cell, with up to half of the daily methionine intake in humans used for SAM synthesis, the vast majority of which is used for methylation (Lu, 2000).
evidence: This is cited from a specific reference.

claim: De novo purine synthesis consumes a considerable amount of energy (six ATP for one IMP molecule) and takes 11 steps to produce IMP from the initial ribose-5-phosphate.
source: However, this consumes a considerable amount of energy (six ATP for one IMP molecule) and takes 11 steps to produce IMP from the initial ribose-5-phosphate.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge.

claim: ATP synthesis from adenosine via AMP and ADP is significantly increased in activated rat peritoneal macrophages.
source: This is in line with ATP synthesis from adenosine via AMP and ADP shown to be significantly increased in activated rat peritoneal macrophages (Barankiewicz and Cohen, 1985).
evidence: This is cited from a specific reference.

claim: Adenosine kinase has been shown to be coupled with Ahcy to effectively remove adenosine and keep the SAM transmethylation pathway running.
source: Adenosine kinase has been shown to be coupled with Ahcy to effectively remove adenosine and keep the SAM transmethylation pathway running (Moffatt et al., 2002; Xu et al., 2017; Murugan et al., 2021).
evidence: This is cited from multiple references.

claim: Adenylate kinase is crucial for cellular energy homeostasis, by regulating nucleotides ratio, AMP production and direction to diverse metabolic sensors.
source: Adenylate kinase is crucial for cellular energy homeostasis, by regulating nucleotides ratio, AMP production and direction to diverse metabolic sensors (e.g. AMPK).
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge.

claim: Adenylate kinase is responsible for the transfer of ATP-energy-rich phosphoryl between energy producing and energy utilizing sites by a sequence of repeated reactions, creating an effective energy transfer shuttle across the cell.
source: In addition, it is responsible for the transfer of ATP-energy-rich phosphoryl between energy producing and energy utilizing sites by a sequence of repeated reactions, creating an effective energy transfer shuttle across the cell (Zeleznikar et al., 1990; Zeleznikar et al., 1995; Dzeja et al., 2007; Dzeja and Terzic, 2009).
evidence: This is cited from multiple references.

claim: Drosophila Adk3 and Ak1 are expressed at low levels in quiescent hemocytes, but their expression increases dramatically during infection.
source: Our hemocyte RNAseq and qPCR data show that Drosophila Adk3 and Ak1 are expressed at low levels in quiescent hemocytes, but their expression increases dramatically during infection.
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq and qPCR data.

claim: Experiments using 13C-labeled adenosine show its incorporation into AMP, ADP, ATP, and especially into SAM, in which the incorporation is significantly increased upon hemocyte activation.
source: Experiments using 13C-labeled adenosine show its incorporation into AMP, ADP, ATP, and especially into SAM, in which the incorporation is significantly increased upon hemocyte activation.
evidence: This is supported by isotope tracing data.

claim: Without infection, the methylation index of Adk3 and Ak1 RNAi in hemocytes is the same as in control cells.
source: Without infection, the methylation index of Adk3 and Ak1 RNAi in hemocytes is the same as in control cells.
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data.

claim: Upon infection, there is no increase in the methylation index in Adk3 and Ak1 RNAi cells.
source: However, upon infection, there is no increase in the methylation index in Adk3 and Ak1 RNAi cells.
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data.

claim: The adenosine-induced developmental delay during infection is reduced in Adk3 and Ak1 RNAi.
source: When the SAM transmethylation pathway is not accelerated, Ahcy does not produce more adenosine, and consequently the adenosine-induced developmental delay during infection is reduced in Adk3 and Ak1 RNAi
evidence: This is supported by developmental timing data.

claim: Without infection, Adk3 and Ak1 RNAi larvae develop at the same rate as controls.
source: whereas without infection, RNAi larvae develop at the same rate as controls.
evidence: This is supported by developmental timing data.

claim: Adk3 and Ak1 RNAi in hemocytes negatively affects immune response efficiency.
source: Similar to Ahcy RNAi, Adk3 and Ak1 RNAi in hemocytes also negatively affects immune response efficiency.
evidence: This is supported by lamellocyte counts and survival data.

claim: There is a significant decrease in lamellocytes number in infected Adk3 and Ak1 knockdown larvae.
source: We see a significant decrease in lamellocytes number in our infected knockdown larvae, resulting in decreased survival.
evidence: This is supported by lamellocyte counts and survival data.

claim: Under energy demanding conditions, as during the activation of immune cells, Adk and cytosolic Ak activities appear to support SAM transmethylation pathway activity.
source: At least under energy demanding conditions, as during the activation of immune cells, Adk and cytosolic Ak activities appear to support SAM transmethylation pathway activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: If there are enough nutrients to maintain high levels of ATP, adenosine can be recycled first to AMP by adenosine kinase, then to ADP by adenylate kinase, and finally to ATP by glycolysis.
source: If there are enough nutrients (cell on the left) to maintain high levels of ATP, adenosine can be recycled first to AMP by adenosine kinase, which requires the first ATP, then to ADP by adenylate kinase, which requires the second ATP, and finally to ATP by glycolysis (or oxidative phosphorylation) using glucose (the gray arrow on the left as thick as the one on the right expresses the balance).
evidence: This is part of the hypothetical model illustrated in Figure 6.

claim: If there are not enough nutrients to regenerate ATP from ADP, ATP is produced from two ADP molecules by adenylate kinase, simultaneously generating AMP.
source: If there are not enough nutrients (cell on the right, thin gray arrow on the left) to regenerate ATP from ADP, ATP is produced from two ADP molecules by adenylate kinase, simultaneously generating AMP.
evidence: This is part of the hypothetical model illustrated in Figure 6.

claim: Accumulated AMP prevents adenosine recycling by adenosine kinase.
source: Accumulated AMP prevents adenosine recycling by adenosine kinase (thin gray arrow on the left), and on the contrary, more adenosine can be produced from AMP by 5'nucleotidase.
evidence: This is part of the hypothetical model illustrated in Figure 6.

claim: When adenosine is not recycled, it is pushed out of the cell via the equilibrative nucleoside transporter (ENT) and becomes an extracellular signaling molecule.
source: In this case, adenosine is pushed out of the cell (thick gray arrow down) via the equilibrative nucleoside transporter (ENT) and becomes an extracellular signaling molecule.
evidence: This is part of the hypothetical model illustrated in Figure 6.
